analysis.one_liner: Eliminates the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, the federal watchdog for consumer finance.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 66 House Republicans, was referred to the Financial Services Committee in July 2015 and never received a markup or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would repeal the section of the 2010 Dodd-Frank law that created the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, abolishing the agency outright. The CFPB is the federal regulator that handles consumer complaints and writes and enforces rules for credit cards, mortgages, checking accounts, payday loans, debt collection, and credit reports. Repealing it would return consumer finance oversight to the scattered arrangement that existed before the 2008 financial crisis.
analysis.who_benefits: If the bill passed, banks, credit card issuers, mortgage lenders, payday lenders, debt collectors, and credit reporting agencies would gain: the single agency that supervises them, writes consumer protection rules, and pursues enforcement against them for consumer refunds and penalties would cease to exist, leaving only the weaker pre-2010 regulatory structure.

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals the Consumer Financial Protection Act of 2010 and restores the law as it stood before that act, which would abolish the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau.

Eliminating the bureau would end its dedicated supervision and rulewriting over consumer financial products and its enforcement actions that have obtained refunds and penalties for consumers from banks and lenders.

analysis.who_pays: Consumers would bear the cost. Anyone with a credit card, mortgage, checking account, student loan, payday loan, debt in collection, or credit report would lose the one federal agency built specifically to take their complaints and police lenders; disputes would fall back to fragmented, industry-facing regulators that predated the 2010 law.

drawbacks.text: Repeal would abolish the bureau's complaint system, supervision, and rulemaking across credit cards, mortgages, payday loans, debt collection, and credit reporting, leaving no dedicated federal consumer finance regulator.

The repeal would revive the pre-2010 legal framework, meaning consumer disputes would return to the fragmented regulators that existed before the 2008 financial crisis, none of which had consumer protection as their primary mission.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Sponsors' stated rationale is removing an agency they view as unaccountable, and regulated firms would save compliance costs. But those savings are concentrated on the industry being policed, while the loss of a dedicated consumer watchdog spreads across tens of millions of households in the form of weaker complaint handling, fewer refunds, and less policing of lending and debt collection practices. On balance, the costs to ordinary consumers outweigh the benefits, which flow mainly to the financial industry.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the House Financial Services Committee, which never took it up, and it died when the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.

narrative.text: Rep. John Ratcliffe introduced the bill on July 20, 2015, with 65 Republican cosponsors, to repeal Title X of Dodd-Frank and eliminate the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services the same day.
No further action was taken: the committee never held a markup or vote, the bill never reached the House floor, and it expired when the Congress ended on January 3, 2017.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Consumers are better off because the bill died: the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau kept operating with its complaint system, supervision, and enforcement powers intact. The banks, lenders, and debt collectors the bureau polices did not get the watchdog removed.

for.name: Rep. John Ratcliffe
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the law creating the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau.

for.name: 65 of 247 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill to eliminate the CFPB.

against.name: Jeb Hensarling
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a committee markup or vote; the committee took no action on it during the two-year Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 66 sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrat signed on to the bill.

industries.note: The bill would remove the CFPB, the agency that supervises banks and card issuers and enforces rules on fees, disclosures, and deceptive practices, saving them compliance and enforcement costs at consumers' expense.
These lenders were facing CFPB rulemaking on repeat lending and ability-to-repay standards; abolishing the bureau would remove the regulator best positioned to restrict their practices.

industries.industry: Debt collectors and credit reporting agencies
industries.note: The CFPB is the primary federal enforcer over debt collection and credit reporting; repeal would eliminate dedicated oversight of industries consumers complain about most.
